newsitem.title: GERMANY: BASF to appeal to Bonn on planned Kali&Salz sale.
newsitem.headline: BASF to appeal to Bonn on planned Kali&Salz sale.

text.p: Germany's BASF AG on Wednesday held out hope that Bonn's economics minister might overrule a cartel office decision and thus allow the sale of its stake in Kali & Salz Beteiligungs AG to the world's largest potash producer.
"As paradoxical as it may sound, I see a chance in the monopoly commission's study," BASF board member Gerhard Wolf told a news conference on the eve of a public hearing at the Bonn ministry.
BASF plans to argue the proposed deal will have a positive effect on employment which would far outweigh any concerns about competition harboured by a federal agency.

Thursday's public meeting in Bonn marks a high point in BASF's nearly one year-long struggle to sell its 51 percent stake in German potash producer Kali & Salz to Canada's Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan Inc (PCS).
But neither company expects a quick decision from the ministry.

BASF and PCS appealed to Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt as a last resort after Germany's cartel office had rejected the proposed deal saying the merger would further strengthen K&S's already strong position in the domestic market.
A monopoly commission delivered a report with similar findings.

But BASF and PCS have argued the cartel office's ruling and the commission's report focused too strongly on the competition aspect, largely ignoring the deal's positive knock-on effect for employment.

Not only is Kali & Salz expected to employ some 7,500 people but it is also expected to create a "large number of additional indirectly-related jobs in a region with very high unemployment rates," Wolf said.

For PCS the deal is equally attractive, PCS Chairman Charles Childers said, noting: "PCS does not enter this association with the idea of shutting down K&S mines to allow PCS mines to increase sales...those who have suggested that this is our intention are wrong.

"K&S will continue to operate as a German company, with German executives with its head office in Germany," Childers added. He also stressed PCS had recently made several acquisitions without reducing production but rather increasing it in many cases.
PCS has said it has no alternative targets in mind, should the deal be ultimately rejected, and BASF has not said how they might proceed.
But both companies admitted that this deal has become far more problematic than either of them had imagined.
